name: Janssen
vendor: Janssen Project (Linux Foundation), based on the Gluu Server

foundation.via: A self-funded project chartered directly under the Linux Foundation; Gluu leads day-to-day development

summary: A self-hosted identity and access management server: a certified OpenID Connect provider and OAuth 2.0 authorization server with FIDO2, SCIM and a self-service portal, plus Cedarling, an embeddable policy engine built on Cedar.
intro: At the centre of Janssen is the Auth Server, a Java OAuth 2.0 authorization server and certified OpenID Connect provider. Applications send users to its `/jans-auth/restv1/authorize` endpoint, discover the rest from `/.well-known/openid-configuration`, and receive ID and access tokens; it also implements UMA 2.0 for user-managed access. Around it sit a FIDO2 server for passkeys and security keys, a SCIM server for provisioning users from other systems, Casa, a self-service portal where users enrol second factors, reset passwords and manage consent, and Agama, a designer for multi-step login flows such as identity proofing or step-up authentication. The Config API, a command-line client and a terminal UI configure all of it. Together these are packaged as the Janssen Server.

Data lives in MySQL, the default for production on Kubernetes, PostgreSQL or Amazon Aurora. Production deployments use Helm charts on Kubernetes; Docker images and VM packages for Ubuntu, SUSE and Red Hat are meant for testing. For authorization inside applications Janssen adds Cedarling, a policy decision point written in Rust on Amazon’s Cedar engine: it validates the JWTs an app already holds, maps their claims to Cedar entities and decides in under a millisecond whether an action is allowed, embedded in a browser through WebAssembly or in Java, Go, Python, iOS and Android apps. Gluu, the company that leads development, sells Gluu Flex and Gluu Solo, commercial distributions built on Janssen components.
strengths: One self-hosted server for OpenID Connect, OAuth 2.0, UMA, FIDO2 passkeys and SCIM provisioning, with a self-service portal for users
OpenID certified, inheriting the Gluu Server’s record of passing more OpenID self-certification tests than any other platform
Built for Kubernetes: Helm charts, horizontal scaling and a stated throughput above a billion authentications a day for Gluu-based deployments
Cedarling brings token-based, policy-as-code authorization into the app itself, even into the browser
limits: A large Java system with many services to run, configure and upgrade; Docker and VM installs are documented as for testing only
A small community for a project of this scope: the main repository had about 650 GitHub stars in October 2026, and day-to-day development is led by one company, Gluu
Some parts are still incubating, such as Jans Lock (central authorization built on Cedarling) and the Tarp test client
Running your own identity provider means owning its security patches, key rotation and availability, work a hosted service such as Auth0 does for you

items.name: Auth Server
items.text: The authorization server and OpenID provider, written in Java, and the upstream core of Gluu Flex.

items.name: FIDO2 and SCIM
items.text: Separate services for registering and checking FIDO2 authenticators and for creating and updating users over the SCIM standard.

items.name: Casa and Agama
items.text: Casa is a self-service portal for second factors, password reset and consent; Agama is a drag-and-drop designer for complex authentication flows.

items.name: Cedarling
items.text: An embeddable policy decision point in Rust on the Cedar engine, under 2 MB, with WebAssembly, Java, Go, Python, C, iOS and Android bindings; it can also run as a sidecar or central service.

story: Gluu built the Gluu Server, an open-source identity platform, and by 2020 it had passed more OpenID self-certification tests than any other, and Gluu-based software had shown throughput of more than a billion authentications a day. Its CEO, Mike Schwartz, explained handing the code to a neutral foundation with the line “trust and security are not competitive advantages”.

On December 8, 2020 the Linux Foundation announced the Janssen Project, built on the code that powers the Gluu Server, with a Technical Steering Committee chaired by Schwartz and including engineers from F5 (NGINX), Santander, IDEMIA, Couchbase and BioID. The project is self-funded and chartered directly under the Linux Foundation, while Gluu leads day-to-day development and sells commercial distributions, Gluu Flex and Gluu Solo, built on it.
Since then the project has moved beyond login. Cedarling, a policy decision point on Amazon’s Cedar language, brings authorization into applications, and v2.5.0 came out on October 7, 2026.

choices.choice: Move the code to the Linux Foundation, keep the product at Gluu
choices.why: A neutral home lets competitors and customers contribute to shared identity infrastructure, while Gluu earns money from supported distributions built on it.
The project relies on Kubernetes autoscaling and newer persistence options to handle concurrency, so Helm is the production deployment and VM installs are for testing.

choices.choice: Authorization from tokens, at the app
choices.why: Cedarling evaluates Cedar policies against the JWTs an application already has, without fetching data during a decision, so checks are fast enough to run inside the app or browser.
